Item 1.01. Entry into a Material Definitive Agreement.
On November 17, 2026, 1011778 B.C. Unlimited Liability Company, an unlimited liability company organized under the laws of British Columbia (the “Issuer”), and New Red Finance, Inc., a Delaware corporation and a direct wholly owned subsidiary of the Issuer (the “Co-Issuer” and, together with the Issuer, the “Issuers”), each a subsidiary of Restaurant Brands International Inc., a corporation organized under the laws of Canada (the “Company”), and the Guarantors (as defined below) entered into an underwriting agreement (the “Underwriting Agreement”) with J.P. Morgan Securities LLC, Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC and RBC Capital Markets, LLC, as representatives of the several underwriters listed in Schedule 1 thereto (the “Underwriters”), relating to the public offering (the “Offering”) by the Issuers of $500.0 million aggregate principal amount of their 6.000% Senior Secured Notes due 2031 (the “2031 Notes”) and $500.0 million aggregate principal amount of their 6.400% Senior Secured Notes due 2036 (the “2036 Notes” and, together with the 2031 Notes, the “Notes”). The Offering was made pursuant to an effective shelf registration statement on Form S-3 (including a prospectus dated November 16, 2026 and the related preliminary prospectus supplement dated November 16, 2026 (the “Prospectus Supplement”)) filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission pursuant to the Securities Act of 1933, as amended, on November 16, 2026.
The Issuers expect to use the proceeds from the Offering to repay a portion of outstanding borrowings under the Issuers’ term loan B facility and to pay fees and expenses in connection therewith and the Offering.
The Notes will be senior secured obligations of the Issuers, guaranteed fully and unconditionally, and jointly and
severally, (i) on a senior unsecured basis by the Company and (ii) on a first lien senior secured basis by Restaurant Brands International Limited Partnership (the “Partnership”) and certain of its wholly-owned subsidiaries (collectively with the Company and the Partnership, the “Guarantors”) that also guarantee the Issuers’ obligations under the Issuers’ existing senior secured credit facilities. The liens securing the notes and the guarantees will be released in the event that RBI achieves a corporate investment grade credit rating from at least two rating agencies. 
The Underwriting Agreement contains customary representations, warranties and covenants by the Issuers and the Guarantors together with customary closing conditions. Under the terms of the Underwriting Agreement, the Issuers and the Guarantors have agreed to indemnify the Underwriters against certain liabilities. The representations, warranties and covenants contained in the Underwriting Agreement were made only for purposes of such agreement and as of the dates specified therein, were solely for the benefit of the parties thereto and may be subject to standards of materiality applicable to the contracting parties that differ from those applicable to investors. Investors should not rely on the representations, warranties and covenants or any descriptions thereof as characterizations of the actual state of facts or condition of the Company and its subsidiaries. Moreover, information concerning the subject matter of any representations, warranties and covenants may change after the date of the Underwriting Agreement, which subsequent information may or may not be fully reflected in public disclosures by the Company. 
As more fully described under the caption “Underwriting (Conflicts of Interest)” in the Prospectus Supplement, certain of the Underwriters and their respective affiliates have provided, and may in the future provide, a variety of these services to the Issuers and to persons and entities with relationships with the Issuers, for which they have received or will receive customary fees and expenses. In particular, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., an affiliate of J.P. Morgan Securities LLC, acts as administrative agent, collateral agent and as a lender under the Issuers’ senior secured credit facilities, and affiliates of certain of the other Underwriters, including Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC and RBC Capital Markets, LLC, act as lenders under the Issuers’ senior secured credit facilities. Affiliates of certain Underwriters also act as lenders under the Issuers’ term loan B facility and thus will receive a portion of the proceeds from the Offering as a result of the partial repayment of the outstanding borrowings under the Issuers’ term loan B facility. The description of the Underwriting Agreement contained in this Item 1.01 does not purport to be complete and is qualified in its entirety by reference to the full text of the Underwriting Agreement. The Underwriting Agreement is filed as Exhibit 1.1 to this Current Report on Form 8-K and its terms are incorporated herein by reference.

Item 3.03 - Material Modification to Rights of Security Holders.
On November 15, 2026, each outstanding share of Class B common stock, par value $0.001 per share (the “Class B Common Stock”), of Rivian Automotive, Inc. (the “Company”), automatically converted (the “Conversion”) into one share of the Company’s Class A common stock, par value $0.001 per share (the “Class A Common Stock”), pursuant to the terms of the Company’s Restated Certificate of Incorporation (the “Certificate of Incorporation”). 
The Conversion occurred pursuant to Article Fourth, Section A.3.1.2 of the Certificate of Incorporation, which provides that each outstanding share of Class B Common Stock will automatically convert into one share of Class A Common Stock at 5:00 p.m. New York City time on the five-year anniversary of the closing of the Company’s initial public offering of Class A Common Stock. As of immediately prior to the Conversion, 7,825,000 shares of Class B Common Stock had been issued, representing the entire number of Class B Common Stock authorized under the Certificate of Incorporation, and 3,912,500 shares of Class B Common Stock remained outstanding, reflecting the prior conversion of 3,912,500 shares of Class B Common Stock to Class A Common Stock pursuant to Article Fourth, Section A.3.1 of the Certificate of Incorporation. Immediately following the Conversion, there were approximately 1,459,886,616 shares of Class A Common Stock outstanding.
Article Fourth, Section A.3.1.4 of the Certificate of Incorporation provides that shares of Class B Common Stock that are converted into shares of Class A Common Stock as provided in Article Fourth, Section A.3.1 of the Certificate of Incorporation will be retired and cancelled and may not be reissued. Following the Conversion, on November 16, 2026, the Company filed a Certificate of Retirement (the “Certificate of Retirement”) with the Secretary of State of the State of Delaware pursuant to Section 243(b) of the Delaware General Corporation Law (the “DGCL”), which effected the retirement of the 7,825,000 shares of Class B Common Stock that were previously issued but no longer outstanding. Pursuant to Section 243(b) of the DGCL, upon its effectiveness, the Certificate of Retirement had the effect of eliminating from the Certificate of Incorporation all references to the Class B Common Stock.
The Conversion had the following effects, among others, on holders of shares of Class B Common Stock: 
•Voting Power. Prior to the Conversion, holders of shares of Class B Common Stock were entitled to cast ten votes per share on any matter submitted to the stockholders of the Company for a vote or approval. As a result of the Conversion, all former holders of shares of Class B Common Stock are now holders of an equal number of shares of Class A Common Stock, which are entitled to cast only one vote per share on matters submitted to the stockholders. In addition, the provisions of the Certificate of Incorporation and Delaware law that entitled the holders of shares of Class A Common Stock and Class B Common Stock, in certain circumstances, to separate class voting rights are no longer applicable as a result of the Conversion.
•Economic Interests. Because holders of shares of Class A Common Stock are entitled to the same economic interests to which former holders of shares of Class B Common Stock were entitled before the Conversion, including with regard to dividends, liquidation rights and treatment in connection with a change of control or merger transaction, the Conversion had no impact on the economic interests of former holders of shares of Class B Common Stock.
•Capitalization. The Conversion had no impact on the total number of the Company’s outstanding shares of capital stock, as the shares of Class B Common Stock converted into an equivalent number of shares of Class A Common Stock. Pursuant to Section 243(b) of the DGCL, the filing of the Certificate of Retirement had the effect of amending the Certificate of Incorporation such that, upon the effectiveness of the Certificate of Retirement, the Company’s total number of authorized shares of capital stock was reduced by 7,825,000, representing the shares of Class B Common Stock retired in connection with the Conversion.
Item 5.03 - Amendments to Articles of Incorporation or Bylaws; Change in Fiscal Year.
As described under Item 3.03, on November 16, 2026, the Company filed the Certificate of Retirement with the Secretary of State of the State of Delaware to effect the retirement of the shares of Class B Common Stock that were issued but not outstanding following the Conversion and to eliminate from the Certificate of Incorporation all references to the Class B Common Stock, pursuant to Section 243(b) of the DGCL. The Company subsequently filed 
a Restated Certificate of Incorporation with the Secretary of State of the State of Delaware on November 17, 2026, incorporating the amendments effected by the Certificate of Retirement (the “Restated Certificate”). 
The above descriptions of the Certificate of Retirement and the Restated Certificate do not purport to be complete and are qualified in their entirety by reference to the full text of the Certificate of Retirement and Restated Certificate, as applicable, which are attached as Exhibit 3.1 and Exhibit 3.2, respectively, and incorporated herein by reference.
Item 8.01 - Other Events.
The Class A Common Stock will continue to trade on The Nasdaq Stock Market under the ticker symbol “RIVN” following the Conversion and will maintain the same CUSIP number previously assigned to the Class A Common Stock.

NVIDIA Announces Financial Results for Third Quarter Fiscal 2027
•Revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year ago
•Data Center revenue of $107.6 billion, up 110% from a year ago
•Vera Rubin NVL72, the most versatile and advanced computing platform ever built, has shipped
SANTA CLARA, Calif.—Nov. 17, 2026―NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today reported revenue for the third quarter ended October 25, 2026, of $115.8 billion, up 20% from the previous quarter and up 103% from a year ago. For the quarter, GAAP and non-GAAP gross margins were 74.8% and 74.9%, respectively. GAAP and non-GAAP earnings per diluted share were $2.70 and $2.68, respectively. 
“Our momentum is real. NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people,” said Colette Kress, interim CEO and executive vice president and chief financial officer of NVIDIA. “Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater.”
In September 2026, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors approved an increase of $150 billion to the company’s share repurchase authorization, without expiration. During the third quarter of fiscal 2027, NVIDIA returned $28.1 billion to shareholders in the form of shares repurchased and cash dividends. As of the end of the third quarter, the company had approximately $227.3 billion remaining under its share repurchase authorization. 
NVIDIA will pay its next quarterly cash dividend of $0.25 per share on December 23, 2026, to all shareholders of record on December 2, 2026.

Outlook
NVIDIA’s outlook for the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, which includes an additional week, is as follows:
•Revenue is expected to be $130.0 billion, plus or minus 3%. NVIDIA is not assuming any Data Center compute revenue from China in its outlook.
•GAAP and non-GAAP gross margins are expected to be between 71.0% and 72.0%. 
•GAAP and non-GAAP operating expenses are expected to be approximately $11.0 billion and $10.7 billion, respectively. 
•For the full year fiscal 2027, NVIDIA expects GAAP and non-GAAP tax rates to be between 16.0% and 18.0%, excluding any discrete items and material changes to NVIDIA’s tax environment.
Highlights
Data Center 
•Third-quarter revenue was $107.6 billion, up 21% from the previous quarter and up 110% from a year ago. 
•Ramped production and began shipping NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 — the fastest product ramp in the company’s history — with racks running at partners including CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Nebius, and coming online soon at SpaceXSI.
•Expanded the Vera Rubin cloud ecosystem, announcing general availability of Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, general availability of Google Cloud’s Vera Rubin-powered A5X instances and the continued buildout of SpaceXSI’s infrastructure. 
•Announced Vera Rubin open architecture advances to help the industry scale faster, and revealed that Cisco, Google, Meta, Microsoft and Visionbay are joining many technology leaders advancing infrastructure for Vera Rubin. 
•Revealed that leading AI natives, cloud providers and neoclouds, including CoreWeave, Meta, Nebius, Nscale, OpenAI and Verda, are building with NVIDIA Vera CPUs to support the growing computing needs of businesses and developers, joining AWS, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and SpaceXSI.
•Expanded Anthropic’s access to NVIDIA Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin capacity through cloud providers, and continued to collaborate on design and engineering to optimize future NVIDIA architectures for Anthropic’s workloads.
•Announced the NVIDIA Vera CPU rack-scale platform for high-performance computing — combining NVIDIA’s first fully custom data center CPU with the gold standard for HPC networking to drive extreme efficiency and throughput for scientific modeling, simulation and agentic science.
•Introduced NVIDIA Rubin HPC, a new GPU in the Vera Rubin platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows. 
•Expanded collaboration with Meta on AI agent Muse and its family of models, with Meta planning expanded deployment of Vera Rubin, Vera CPUs, NVIDIA Spectrum-X™ networking and BlueField®-4 to scale training, inference and agents.
•Introduced DSX POD, a reference design for complete Vera Rubin AI factories built by partners inside modular containers, integrated and validated before delivery to accelerate infrastructure deployment.
•Announced European ecosystem adoption of NVIDIA DSX™ to reduce AI factory power requirements and enable near-zero facility cooling water consumption.
•Announced that NVIDIA swept every MLPerf Training and Endpoints benchmark, and Vera Rubin NVL72 demonstrated leading inference performance in its MLPerf Inference preview debut.
•Launched NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform and introduced the NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture, combining open source OpenShell software, Vera Rubin for model inference, Vera CPUs

Realty
Income Announces Chief Strategy Officer Transition
SAN
DIEGO, CALIFORNIA, November 12, 2026....Realty Income Corporation (Realty Income, NYSE: O), The Monthly Dividend Company®,
today announced that its Executive Vice President and Chief Strategy Officer, and President of Realty Income International, Neil Abraham,
will be leaving the company. To ensure a smooth transition, Mr. Abraham will continue to serve in his current role through December 31,
2026, and Realty Income intends to enter into a consulting agreement with Mr. Abraham through March 31, 2027.
“Neil
has been a valued member of the senior management team and a leader for the company,” said Sumit Roy, Realty Income’s President
and Chief Executive Officer. “On behalf of myself, the Board of Directors and the entire team at Realty Income, we want to thank
Neil for his partnership and contributions to many defining moments for the company over the past 11 years, and we wish him continued
success in his future endeavors.”
“Being
part of Realty Income’s growth has been one of the great joys of my career,” said Neil Abraham. “As I step into a new chapter
and explore fresh opportunities, I leave feeling proud of everything we built together. I’m grateful to my colleagues, the Board and
our partners for their support and trust along the way, and excited to watch Realty Income reach new heights in the years to come.”
About
Realty Income
Realty
Income (NYSE: O), an S&P 500 company, is real estate partner to the world’s leading companies®. Founded in
1969, we serve our clients as a full-service real estate capital provider. As of September 30, 2026, we have a portfolio of over 15,500
properties in all 50 U.S. states, the U.K., and eight other countries in Europe. We are known as “The Monthly Dividend Company®”
and have a mission to invest in people and places to deliver dependable monthly dividends that increase over time. Since our founding,
we have declared 677 consecutive monthly dividends and are a member of the S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats® index for
having increased our dividend for over 32 consecutive years. Additional information about the company can be found at www.realtyincome.com.

Item 5.02 Departure of Directors or Certain Officers; Election of Directors; Appointment of Certain Officers; Compensatory Arrangements of Certain Officers.
On November 13, 2026, Lowe’s Companies, Inc. (the “Company” or “Lowe’s”) appointed Margrethe (Margi) Vagell as Executive Vice President, Merchandising, effective November 14, 2026, succeeding William P. Boltz as part of his planned retirement. Ms. Vagell will also retain her responsibilities for Supply Chain, including the Company’s logistics, distribution centers, transportation and delivery services, and inventory replenishment and planning. Mr. Boltz will work closely with Ms. Vagell in the coming months to support a seamless transition. Following this transition, Mr. Boltz will serve as President of the Lowe’s Foundation (the “Foundation”), effective January 30, 2027. His appointment reinforces his long-standing commitment to the Foundation and its mission to build the skilled trades workforce. These leadership changes are designed to further connect the capabilities the Company has built through its Total Home Strategy and accelerate execution across the business.

Item 5.02. Departure of Directors or Certain Officers; Election of Directors; Appointment of Certain Officers; Compensatory Arrangements of Certain Officers.
 | | | | | | 
 | 
(i) | 
2027 Annual Bonus Plan
On November 17, 2026, upon the recommendation of the Executive Compensation and Human Resources Committee (the “Compensation Committee”), the Board of Directors (the “Board”) of Boston Scientific Corporation (the “Company”) approved the Company’s 2027 Annual Bonus Plan effective for the performance year of January 1, 2027 through December 31, 2027 (the “2027 Annual Bonus Plan”).
As part of the Company’s overall compensation program, the 2027 Annual Bonus Plan provides an annual cash incentive opportunity for eligible exempt and nonexempt indirect labor or equivalent personnel (including the Company’s named executive officers meeting the eligibility criteria) based on the achievement of certain performance metrics. The 2027 Annual Bonus Plan is substantially similar to the 2026 annual bonus plan and provides:
•for the performance year, an aggregate bonus pool equal to the total target annual bonuses of all plan participants multiplied by the applicable distribution percentage, as well a dynamic bonus pool, which shall be equal to 10% or less of the total target annual bonuses for all plan participants; 
•following the end of the performance year, the Compensation Committee shall determine the applicable distribution percentage (between 0% - 150%), based on the Company’s performance measured against Company-wide goals for global sales and adjusted earnings per share; provided the Board maintains its discretion to terminate, suspend or modify the 2027 Annual Bonus Plan and to reduce the applicable distribution percentage based on the Company’s performance relative to its quality objectives and performance of its quality systems; and
•managers will then assign each plan participant under their management an individual performance modifier (between 0% - 150%) based on such participant’s performance, which will be used to determine the participant’s final bonus award, resulting in a maximum payout potential for any individual participant of 0% - 225% of an individual’s target bonus, consistent with prior annual bonus plan years.
Awards to certain executive officers under the 2027 Annual Bonus Plan are subject to (i) the Company’s discretionary recoupment policy, which provides that, to the extent permitted by law, the Company may seek reimbursement of a bonus award in the event of an executive officer’s misconduct or gross dereliction of duty that results in a material violation of Company policy and causes significant harm to the Company and (ii) the Company’s Dodd-Frank Clawback Policy and any other compensation recovery policy adopted by the Board including in response to the requirements of Section 10D of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended (the “Exchange Act”), the final rules of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (the “SEC”) thereunder, and any applicable listing rules or other rules and regulations implementing the foregoing or as otherwise required by law. 
This description of the 2027 Annual Bonus Plan does not purport to be complete and is subject to and qualified in its entirety by reference to the full text of such plan. A copy of the 2027 Annual Bonus Plan is included in this filing as Exhibit 10.1 and incorporated herein by reference.
 | | | | | | 
 | 
(ii) | 
2027 Performance Share Programs
On November 17, 2026, upon the recommendation of the Compensation Committee, the Board approved the adoption of two performance share programs, the Boston Scientific Corporation 2027 Relative Total Shareholder Return Performance Share Program (the “2027 rTSR PSP”) and the Boston Scientific Corporation 2027 Organic Net Sales Growth Performance Share Program (the “2027 Organic Net Sales PSP”). The 2027 rTSR PSP and the 2027 Organic Net Sales PSP are substantially similar to the 2026 Total Shareholder Return Performance Share Program and the 2026 Organic Net Sales Growth Performance Share Program, respectively. These programs represent an important component of the overall mix of the Company’s long-term incentive program. Under both programs, if the relevant program criteria are met, performance share awards will be granted to the Company’s executive officers in the form of restricted stock units issued under the Company’s Amended and Restated 2011 Long-Term Incentive Plan. Awards to certain executive officers under both programs are subject to (i) the Company’s discretionary recoupment policy, which provides that, to the extent permitted by law, the Company may seek recovery of performance share units in the event of an executive officer’s misconduct or gross dereliction of duty that results in a material violation of Company policy and causes significant harm to the Company, and (ii) the Company’s Dodd-Frank Clawback Policy and any other compensation recovery policy adopted by the Board including in response to the requirements of Section 10D of the Exchange Act, the final rules of the SEC thereunder, and any applicable listing rules or other rules and regulations implementing the foregoing or as otherwise required by law.
 | | | | | | 
 | 
(A) | 
2027 Relative Total Shareholder Return Performance Share Program
The purpose of the 2027 rTSR PSP is to align the Company’s executive compensation program with the interests of stockholders and to reinforce the concept of pay for performance by comparing the Total Shareholder Return (“TSR”) of the Company’s common stock to the TSR of the other companies included in the S&P 500 Healthcare Index over a three-year period beginning on January 1, 2027 and ending on December 31, 2029 (the “Performance Period”). The number of performance shares awarded will be in a range of 0% to 200% of each participant’s target number of awards based on the Company’s TSR rank. Performance share awards will vest only upon satisfaction of both the performance criteria and the payment eligibility criteria set forth in the 2027 rTSR PSP, subject to certain exceptions in the event of a change of control or termination for retirement, death or disability. In the event a participant’s employment with the Company terminates due to retirement, as defined therein, prior to January 1, 2028, the performance share awards will be forfeited in their entirety.
This description of the 2027 rTSR PSP does not purport to be complete and is subject to and qualified in its entirety by reference to the full text of such program. A copy of the 2027 rTSR PSP is included in this filing as Exhibit 10.2 and incorporated herein by reference.
 (B) 2027 Organic Net Sales Growth Performance Share Program
The purpose of the 2027 Organic Net Sales PSP is to align the Company’s executive compensation program with the interests of stockholders and to reinforce the concept of pay for performance by providing incentives for the achievement of key business performance objectives critical to the Company’s success. Under the 2027 Organic Net Sales PSP, performance will be measured by comparing the Company’s organic net sales growth, for the three-year period beginning on January 1, 2027 and ending on December 31, 2029 against its financial plan performance for organic net sales, as defined by the 2027 Organic Net Sales PSP. Organic net sales growth, as defined under the 2027 Organic Net Sales PSP, is net sales excluding the impact of foreign currency fluctuation and the impact of certain acquisitions and divestitures for which there are less than a full period of comparable net sales. The number of performance shares awarded will be in a range of 0% to 200% of each participant’s target number of awards, depending on such performance. Performance share awards will only vest upon satisfaction of both the performance criteria and the payment eligibility criteria set forth in the 2027 Organic Net Sales PSP, subject to certain exceptions in the event of a change of control or termination for retirement, death or disability. Item 1.01. Entry into a Material Definitive Agreement. 
On November 17, 2026 (the “Issue Date”), Cheniere Energy, Inc. (“Cheniere”) closed the sale of its previously announced offering of $1.2 billion aggregate principal amount of 5.800% Senior Notes due 2037 (the “Notes”). The Notes were issued at 99.313% of par. The sale of the Notes was not registered under the Securities Act of 1933, as amended (the “Securities Act”), and the Notes were sold in reliance on Rule 144A and Regulation S thereunder. 
Indenture 
The Notes were issued on the Issue Date pursuant to an indenture, dated as of March 19, 2026 (the “Base Indenture”), by and between Cheniere and The Bank of New York Mellon, as trustee (the “Trustee”), as supplemented by the third supplemental indenture, dated as of the Issue Date, between Cheniere and the Trustee, relating to the Notes (the “Third Supplemental Indenture”). The Base Indenture as supplemented by the Third Supplemental Indenture is referred to herein as the “Notes Indenture.” 
Under the terms of the Third Supplemental Indenture, the Notes will mature on March 15, 2037 and will accrue interest at a rate equal to 5.800% per annum on the principal amount from the Issue Date, with such interest payable semi-annually, in cash in arrears, on March 15 and September 15 of each year, beginning on March 15, 2027. 
The Notes are Cheniere’s senior unsubordinated obligations, ranking equally in right of payment with Cheniere’s other existing and future senior unsubordinated debt and senior in right of payment to any of Cheniere’s future subordinated debt. The Notes are not initially guaranteed by any of Cheniere’s subsidiaries. In the future, any subsidiary that guarantees or becomes a co-obligor with respect to any obligations of Cheniere in respect of Cheniere’s existing 4.625% senior notes due 2028 will also guarantee the Notes. 
At any time or from time to time prior to September 15, 2036 (the “Par Call Date”), Cheniere may, at its option, redeem all or part of the Notes at a redemption price equal to the greater of (i) 100% of the principal amount of the Notes to be redeemed and (ii) a specified make-whole redemption price set forth in the Third Supplemental Indenture, in either case plus accrued and unpaid interest to the redemption date. On and after the Par Call Date, Cheniere may redeem the Notes at its option, in whole at any time or in part from time to time at a redemption price equal to 100% of the principal amount of the Notes redeemed plus accrued and unpaid interest, if any, to (but not including) the applicable redemption date. 
The Notes Indenture also contains customary terms and events of default and certain covenants that, among other things, limit Cheniere’s ability to incur liens, enter into sale-leaseback transactions and consolidate, merge or sell, lease or otherwise dispose of all or substantially all of Cheniere’s properties or assets. The Notes Indenture covenants are subject to a number of important limitations and exceptions. 
The foregoing description of the Base Indenture is qualified in its entirety by reference to the full text of the Base Indenture, a copy of which is filed as Exhibit 4.1 to Cheniere’s Current Report on Form 8-K filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (the “SEC”) on March 19, 2026 and is incorporated by reference herein. The foregoing description of the Third Supplemental 
Indenture is qualified in its entirety by reference to the full text of the Third Supplemental Indenture, a copy of which is filed as Exhibit 4.2 hereto and is incorporated by reference herein. Any capitalized terms used herein and not otherwise defined have the meaning ascribed to them in the Notes Indenture. 
Registration Rights Agreement 
In connection with the issuance of the Notes, Cheniere and Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC, as representative of the initial purchasers, entered into a Registration Rights Agreement dated as of the Issue Date (the “Registration Rights Agreement”). Under the terms of the Registration Rights Agreement, Cheniere has agreed to use commercially reasonable efforts to file with the SEC and cause to become effective a registration statement with respect to an offer to exchange any or all of the Notes, for a like aggregate principal amount of debt securities of Cheniere issued under the Notes Indenture and identical in all material respects to the respective Notes sought to be exchanged (other than with respect to restrictions on transfer or to any increase in annual interest rate), and that are registered under the Securities Act. Cheniere has agreed to use commercially reasonable efforts to cause such registration statement to become effective within 360 days after the Issue Date. Under specified circumstances, Cheniere has also agreed to use commercially reasonable efforts to cause to become effective a shelf registration statement relating to resales of the Notes. Cheniere will be obligated to pay additional interest if it fails to comply with its obligations to register the Notes within the specified time periods. 
This description of the Registration Rights Agreement is qualified in its entirety by reference to the full text of the Registration Rights Agreement, a copy of which is filed as Exhibit 10.1 hereto and is incorporated by reference herein.

 | Item 8.01. | 
Other Events.
On November 12, 2026, The Southern Company (the “Company”) entered into an underwriting agreement (the “Underwriting Agreement”) with the underwriters named in Schedule I thereto (the “Underwriters”), for whom BofA Securities, Inc. and Barclays Capital Inc. are acting as representatives, covering the issuance and sale of 35,000,000 equity units, initially in the form of corporate units (the “Corporate Units”). Pursuant to the Underwriting Agreement, the Company also granted the Underwriters an option to purchase up to an additional 5,000,000 Corporate Units to cover over-allotments. On November 17, 2026, the Company completed its offering of the 40,000,000 Corporate Units, including the exercise in full of the Underwriters’ over-allotment option.
Each Corporate Unit has a stated amount of $50 and is comprised of (i) a purchase contract (each, a “stock purchase contract”) which will obligate the holder to purchase from the Company, no later than December 15, 2029 (or, if such day is not a business day, on the following business day), a certain number of shares of the Company’s common stock, $0.01 par value (the “Common Stock”), for $50 in cash; (ii) a 1/40 undivided beneficial ownership interest in $1,000 principal amount of the Company’s Series 2026C Remarketable Senior Notes due 2031 (the “Series 2026C RSNs”); and (iii) a 1/40 undivided beneficial ownership interest in $1,000 principal amount of the Company’s Series 2026D Remarketable Senior Notes due 2034 (the “Series 2026D RSNs” and, together with the Series 2026C RSNs, the “RSNs”). Total annual distributions on the Corporate Units will be at the rate of 8.625% of the stated amount, consisting of quarterly contract adjustment payments under the stock purchase contracts in the amount of 3.125% per year and interest on the RSNs in the amount of 5.50% per year.
The RSNs were issued pursuant to the Senior Note Indenture, dated as of June 1, 2026 (the “Senior Note Indenture”), between the Company and U.S. Bank Trust Company, National Association, as trustee, as supplemented, including by a Third Supplemental Indenture and a Fourth Supplemental Indenture, each dated as of November 17, 2026.
The stock purchase contracts were issued pursuant to a Purchase Contract and Pledge Agreement dated as of November 17, 2026 (the “Purchase Contract and Pledge Agreement”), between the Company and U.S. Bank Trust Company, National Association, in its capacity as the purchase contract agent, collateral agent, custodial agent and securities intermediary.
Under the terms of the Purchase Contract and Pledge Agreement, the RSNs are pledged as collateral to secure the obligations of the holders of the Corporate Units to purchase the shares of Common Stock under the stock purchase contracts that form a part of the Corporate Units. Each of the RSNs will be remarketed, subject to certain terms and conditions, prior to the applicable stock purchase contract settlement date pursuant to the terms of the Purchase Contact and Pledge Agreement and a remarketing agreement to be entered into among the Company, U.S. Bank Trust Company, National Association and a remarketing agent.
The Corporate Units were registered under the Securities Act of 1933, as amended, pursuant to the shelf registration statement (Registration No. 333-296531) of the Company.
The foregoing disclosure is qualified in its entirety by reference to the Underwriting Agreement which is attached hereto as Exhibit 1.7, the Senior Note Indenture previously filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the Third Supplemental Indenture, which is attached hereto as Exhibit 4.3(a), the Fourth Supplemental Indenture, which is attached hereto as Exhibit 4.3(b), the form of Series 2026C RSN, which is included in Exhibit 4.3(a) hereto, the form of Series 2026D RSN, which is included in Exhibit 4.3(b) hereto, the Purchase Contract and Pledge Agreement, which is attached hereto as Exhibit 4.12, and the forms of Remarketing Agreement, Corporate Unit and Treasury Unit, each of which is included in Exhibit 4.12 hereto.

Technical information: (202) 691-7000 * cpi_info@bls.gov * www.bls.gov/cpi
Media contact: (202) 691-5902 * PressOffice@bls.gov 
CONSUMER PRICE INDEX - OCTOBER 2026
The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) increased 0.4 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis in October 
after rising 0.6 percent in September, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. 
The index for shelter rose 0.3 percent in October, accounting for over thirty percent of the monthly all items increase. 
The food index increased 0.5 percent in October, as the food at home index rose 0.4 percent and the food away from home 
index increased 0.5 percent. The index for energy increased 0.7 percent over the month following a 5.2-percent increase 
in September. 
The index for all items less food and energy rose 0.3 percent in October, as it did in September and August. Indexes that 
increased over the month include recreation, medical care, motor vehicle insurance, household furnishings and operations, 
and education. Conversely, the index for used cars and trucks and the index for communication were among the small number 
of major indexes that decreased in October.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 October 2026 12-Month Percent Changes
BLS did not collect survey data for October 2025 because of a lapse in appropriations. For most CPI series, 
BLS could not publish October 2025 indexes. As a result, BLS cannot publish 12-month percent changes for 
October 2026 for indexes where October 2025 data are unavailable. Information about handling missing data is 
available online at www.bls.gov/cpi/factsheets/approximating-missing-data.htm

Food
The index for food rose 0.5 percent in October after being unchanged in September. The food at home index increased 0.4 
percent over the month. Four of the six major grocery store food group indexes increased in October, while one index 
decreased. The index for other food at home increased 0.7 percent in October, as the index for snacks rose 1.0 percent. 
The meats, poultry, fish, and eggs index increased 0.5 percent over the month, as the beef index rose 0.9 percent. The 
index for fruits and vegetables and the index for dairy and related products each increased 0.6 percent in October. 
In contrast, the nonalcoholic beverages index decreased 0.3 percent in October, after rising 0.9 percent in September. 
The index for cereals and bakery products was unchanged over the month.
The food away from home index rose 0.5 percent in October. The index for full service meals rose 0.7 percent, and the 
index for limited service meals increased 0.4 percent over the month.
Energy
The index for energy increased 0.7 percent in October after rising 5.2 percent in September. The gasoline index increased 
1.0 percent over the month, after advancing 9.1 percent the previous month. (Before seasonal adjustment, gasoline prices 
decreased 0.7 percent in October.) The index for electricity rose 0.9 percent over the month. In contrast, the natural 
gas index decreased 0.8 percent in October.
All items less food and energy
The index for all items less food and energy rose 0.3 percent in October, as it did in September and August. The shelter 
index increased 0.3 percent over the month after rising 0.4 percent in September. The index for owners' equivalent rent 
rose 0.3 percent in October, and the index for rent increased 0.2 percent. The lodging away from home index rose 0.6 
percent in October after rising 2.0 percent the previous month.
The index for recreation increased 0.8 percent over the month after rising 0.5 percent in September. The motor vehicle 
insurance index rose 0.7 percent in October, and the household furnishings and operations index increased 0.2 percent. 
The index for education increased 0.3 percent in October, and the index for new vehicles rose 0.2 percent. The personal 
care index, the airline fares index, and the apparel index also increased over the month.
The medical care index increased 0.3 percent in October after rising 0.1 percent in September. The index for hospital 
services rose 0.8 percent over the month, and the index for physicians' services increased 0.4 percent. The prescription 
drugs index rose 0.3 percent in October. 
The index for used cars and trucks declined 1.2 percent in October after rising 0.7 percent in September. The 
communication index decreased 0.1 percent over the month.
Not seasonally adjusted CPI measures
The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) increased to an index level of 337.511 (1982-84=100). For the 
month, the index rose 0.2 percent prior to seasonal adjustment. 
The Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) increased to an index level of 331.147 
(1982-84=100). For the month, the index increased 0.1 percent prior to seasonal adjustment. 
For the month, the Chained Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (C-CPI-U) increased 0.2 percent on a not 
seasonally adjusted basis. Please note that the indexes for the past 10 to 12 months are subject to revision. 
_______________
The Consumer Price Index news release for November 2026 is scheduled to be published on Thursday, December 10, 2026, 
at 8:30 a.m. (ET).
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Upcoming Consumer Price Index Publication Changes
With the publication of January 2027 CPI data on February 11, 2027, several index titles will change: 
"wireless telephone services" will change to "wireless telephone service"; "physicians' services" will change 
to "physician services"; and "music instruments and accessories" will change to "music instruments and 
accessories including instrument rentals." More information is available online at 
www.bls.gov/cpi/additional-resources/series-title-changes.htm
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Technical Note
Brief Explanation of the CPI
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures the change in prices paid by consumers for goods and services. The CPI reflects
spending patterns for each of two population groups: all urban consumers and urban wage earners and clerical workers.
The all urban consumer group represents over 90 percent of the total U.S. population. It is based on the expenditures
of almost all residents of urban or metropolitan areas, including professionals, the self-employed, the poor, the
unemployed, and retired people, as well as urban wage earners and clerical workers. Not included in the CPI are the
spending patterns of people living in rural nonmetropolitan areas, farming families, people in the Armed Forces, and
those in institutions, such as prisons and mental hospitals. Consumer inflation for all urban consumers is measured by
two indexes, namely, the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) and the Chained Consumer Price Index for
All Urban Consumers (C-CPI-U). 
The Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) is based on the expenditures of households
included in the CPI-U definition that meet two requirements: more than one-half of the household's income must come
from clerical or wage occupations, and at least one of the household's earners must have been employed for at least 37
weeks during the previous 12 months. The CPI-W population represents approximately 30 percent of the total U.S.
population and is a subset of the CPI-U population.
The CPIs are based on prices of food, clothing, shelter, fuels, transportation, doctors' and dentists' services, drugs,
and other goods and services that people buy for day-to-day living. Prices are collected each month in 75 urban areas
across the country from about 6,000 housing units and approximately 22,000 retail establishments (department stores,
supermarkets, hospitals, and other types of stores and service establishments). All taxes directly associated with the
purchase and use of items are included in the index. Prices of fuels and a few other items are obtained every month in
all 75 locations. Prices of most other commodities and services are collected every month in the three largest
geographic areas and every other month in other areas. Prices of most goods and services are obtained by personal
visit, telephone call, web, or app collection by the Bureau's trained representatives.
In calculating the index, price changes for the various items in each location are aggregated using weights, which
represent their importance in the spending of the appropriate population group. Local data are then combined to obtain
a U.S. city average. For the CPI-U and CPI-W, separate indexes are also published by size of city, by region of the
country, for cross-classifications of regions and population-size classes, and for 23 selected local areas. Area
indexes do not measure differences in the level of prices among cities; they only measure the average change in prices
for each area since the base period. For the C-CPI-U, data are issued only at the national level. The CPI-U and CPI-W
are considered final when released, but the C-CPI-U is issued in preliminary form and subject to three subsequent
quarterly revisions. 
The index measures price change from a designed reference date. For most of the CPI-U and the CPI-W, the reference base
is 1982-84 equals 100. The reference base for the C-CPI-U is

Media contact: (202) 691-5902 * PressOffice@bls.gov 
 THE EMPLOYMENT SITUATION - OCTOBER 2026 
Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, and the unemployment rate changed 
little at 4.1 percent, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Employment increased in 
professional and business services, in health care, and in transportation and warehousing. 
This news release presents statistics from two monthly surveys. The household survey measures labor 
force status, including unemployment, by demographic characteristics. The establishment survey 
measures nonfarm employment, hours, and earnings by industry. For more information about the 
concepts and statistical methodology used in these two surveys, see the Technical Note. 
Household Survey Data 
Both the unemployment rate, at 4.1 percent, and the number of unemployed people, at 7.1 million, 
changed little in October. The unemployment rate has remained in a narrow range of 4.1 percent to 
4.3 percent since March. (See table A-1.) 
Among the major worker groups, the unemployment rates showed little or no change in October for 
adult men (3.9 percent), adult women (3.6 percent), teenagers (13.9 percent), and people who are 
White (3.7 percent), Black (6.6 percent), Asian (2.8 percent), or Hispanic (4.7 percent). (See 
tables A-1, A-2, and A-3.) 
The number of long-term unemployed (those jobless for 27 weeks or more), at 2.0 million, changed 
little over the month. The long-term unemployed accounted for 27.6 percent of all unemployed 
people. (See table A-12.) 
Both the labor force participation rate, at 61.9 percent, and the employment-population ratio, at 
59.3 percent, changed little in October. These measures have shown little net change since January. 
(See table A-1.) 
The number of people employed part time for economic reasons increased by 339,000 to 4.8 million in 
October. These individuals would have preferred full-time employment but were working part time 
because their hours had been reduced or they were unable to find full-time jobs. (See table A-8.) 
In October, the number of people not in the labor force who currently want a job changed little at 
6.0 million. These individuals were not counted as unemployed because they were not actively 
looking for work during the 4 weeks preceding the survey or were unavailable to take a job. (See 
table A-1.) 
Among those not in the labor force who wanted a job, the number of people marginally attached to 
the labor force changed little at 1.6 million in October. These individuals wanted and were 
available for work and had looked for a job sometime in the prior 12 months but had not looked for 
work in the 4 weeks preceding the survey. The number of discouraged workers, a subset of the 
marginally attached who believed that no jobs were available for them, also changed little over 
the month at 448,000. (See Summary table A.) 
Establishment Survey Data 
Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, higher than the average monthly gain 
of 48,000 over the prior 12 months. In October, employment increased in professional and business 
services, in health care, and in transportation and warehousing. (See table B-1.) 
Employment in professional and business services increased by 70,000 in October, well above the 
average monthly gain of 15,000 over the prior 12 months. In October, employment continued to trend 
up in professional, scientific, and technical services (+33,000), in administrative and support and 
waste management and remediation services (+28,000), and in management of companies and enterprises 
(+9,000). Professional and business services has added 269,000 jobs since a recent low in October 
2025. 
Health care added 42,000 jobs in October, higher than the average monthly gain of 31,000 over the 
prior 12 months. In October, employment gains occurred in hospitals (+16,000), home health care 
services (+11,000), and outpatient care centers (+5,000). 
In October, transportation and warehousing added 25,000 jobs, reflecting growth in couriers and 
messengers (+17,000) and air transportation (+4,000). Transportation and warehousing has added 
104,000 jobs since a recent employment low in February, with couriers and messengers (+71,000) 
contributing most of the gain. 
Manufacturing employment continued to trend up in October (+19,000) and has increased by 101,000 
since a recent low in December 2025. In October, job gains occurred in computer and electronic 
product manufacturing (+7,000), machinery manufacturing (+4,000), and primary metal manufacturing 
(+4,000). 
Employment showed little change over the month in other major industries, including mining, 
quarrying, and oil and gas extraction; construction; wholesale trade; retail trade; information; 
financial activities; social assistance; leisure and hospitality; other services; and government. 
In October, average hourly earnings for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls increased by 14 
cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38.00. Over the past 12 months, average hourly earnings have increased 
by 3.1 percent. In October, average hourly earnings of private-sector production and nonsupervisory 
employees rose by 12 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $32.75. (See tables B-3 and B-8.) 
The average workweek for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls remained at 34.4 hours in 
October. In manufacturing, the average workweek was unchanged at 40.5 hours, and overtime edged up 
by 0.1 hour to 3.1 hours. The average workweek for production and nonsupervisory employees on 
private nonfarm payrolls declined by 0.1 hour to 33.8 hours. (See tables B-2 and B-7.) 
The change in total nonfarm payroll employment for August was revised up by 53,000, from +133,000 
to +186,000, and the change for September was revised up by 31,000, from +29,000 to +60,000. With 
these revisions, employment in August and September combined is 84,000 higher than previously 
reported. (Monthly revisions result from additional reports received from businesses and government 
agencies since the last published estimates and from the recalculation of seasonal factors.) 
_____________ 
The Employment Situation for November 2026 is scheduled to be published on Friday, December 4, 
2026, at 8:30 a.m. (ET).

 PRODUCER PRICE INDEXES - OCTOBER 2026
The Producer Price Index for final demand rose 0.3 percent in October, seasonally adjusted, the 
U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Final demand prices advanced 1.4 percent in 
September and 0.4 percent in August. (See table A.) On an unadjusted basis, the index for final 
demand increased 6.5 percent for the 12 months ended in October, the largest 12-month rise 
since moving up 7.4 percent in November 2022.
Leading the October advance in final demand prices, the index for final demand goods increased 
0.5 percent. Prices for final demand services moved up 0.2 percent.
The index for final demand less foods, energy, and trade services rose 0.5 percent in October, the 
same as in September. For the 12 months ended in October, prices for final demand less foods, 
energy, and trade services advanced 4.9 percent.
Final Demand
Final demand goods: The index for final demand goods increased 0.5 percent in October following 
a 2.5-percent rise in September. Over 60 percent of the advance in October is attributable to prices 
for final demand goods less foods and energy, which moved up 0.5 percent. The index for final 
demand foods increased 1.3 percent. In contrast, prices for final demand energy edged down 0.1 
percent. For the 12 months ended in October, the index for final demand goods increased 10.2 
percent, the largest 12-month rise since advancing 10.5 percent in October 2022.
Product detail: Within the index for final demand goods in October, prices for basic organic 
chemicals advanced 3.9 percent. The indexes for fresh and dry vegetables; gas fuels; aeronautical, 
nautical, and navigational instruments; jet fuel; and processed young chickens also moved higher. 
(See table 2.) Conversely, diesel fuel prices fell 7.9 percent. The indexes for pork and for passenger 
cars also declined. 
Final demand services: The index for final demand services moved up 0.2 percent in October, the 
fifth consecutive advance. Three-fourths of the October rise can be traced to a 2.0-percent increase in 
prices for final demand transportation and warehousing services. The index for final demand services 
less trade, transportation, and warehousing advanced 0.2 percent. In contrast, margins for final 
demand trade services decreased 0.2 percent.
Product detail: Over 80 percent of the October increase in the index for final demand services is 
attributable to prices for truck transportation of freight, which rose 3.9 percent. The indexes for fuels 
and lubricants retailing; health, beauty, and optical goods retailing; food and alcohol wholesaling; 
hospital outpatient care; and traveler accommodation services also moved higher. Conversely, 
margins for machinery and vehicle wholesaling fell 4.2 percent. Prices for system software 
publishing and for airline passenger services also declined.

Intermediate Demand by Commodity Type
Within intermediate demand in October, the index for processed goods increased 0.4 percent, prices 
for unprocessed goods fell 3.1 percent, and the index for services rose 0.6 percent. (See tables B and 
C.)
Processed goods for intermediate demand: Prices for processed goods for intermediate demand 
advanced 0.4 percent in October, the third consecutive rise. Leading the October increase, the index 
for processed materials less foods and energy moved up 0.9 percent. Prices for processed foods and 
feeds advanced 1.0 percent. In contrast, the index for processed energy goods declined 1.6 percent. 
For the 12 months ended in October, prices for processed goods for intermediate demand increased 
14.6 percent, the largest 12-month rise since jumping 17.2 percent in July 2022.
Product detail: More than 40 percent of the October advance in the index for processed goods for 
intermediate demand can be traced to prices for basic organic chemicals, which moved up 3.9 
percent. The indexes for jet fuel, electronic components and accessories, natural gas liquids, 
fabricated structural metal products, and prepared animal feeds also increased. Conversely, prices for 
diesel fuel fell 7.9 percent. The indexes for pork and for lumber also decreased.
Unprocessed goods for intermediate demand: Prices for unprocessed goods for intermediate 
demand fell 3.1 percent in October, the largest decline since moving down 6.6 percent in June. 
Leading the broad-based decrease in October, the index for unprocessed energy materials dropped 
7.7 percent. Prices for unprocessed nonfood materials less energy and for unprocessed foodstuffs and 
feedstuffs also fell, 0.9 percent and 0.2 percent, respectively. For the 12 months ended in October, the 
index for unprocessed goods for intermediate demand rose 16.9 percent.
Product detail: A major factor in the October decline in the index for unprocessed goods for 
intermediate demand was a 10.3-percent decrease in prices for crude petroleum. The indexes for 
corn, slaughter hogs, wheat, aluminum base scrap, and hay and hayseeds also moved down. In 
contrast, prices for raw milk advanced 8.2 percent. The indexes for natural gas and for carbon steel 
scrap also increased.

REAL EARNINGS  OCTOBER 2026 
All employees 
Real average hourly earnings for all employees were unchanged from September to October, seasonally 
adjusted, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. This result stems from an increase of 0.4 
percent in average hourly earnings combined with an increase of 0.4 percent in the Consumer Price 
Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U). 
Real average weekly earnings were unchanged over the month due to no change in real average hourly 
earnings combined with no change in the average workweek. 
******************************************************************************************************** 
* Federal Government Shutdown * 
* * 
* This release usually includes an over-the-year analysis of changes to real earnings. BLS could not * 
* collect the relevant Consumer Price Index data for the October 2025 reference period due to a lapse * 
* in appropriations in late 2025. For that reason, over-the-year comparisons from October 2025 to * 
* October 2026 are not available. *

******************************************************************************************************** 
Production and nonsupervisory employees 
Real average hourly earnings for production and nonsupervisory employees increased 0.1 percent from 
September to October, seasonally adjusted. This result stems from a 0.4-percent increase in average 
hourly earnings combined with an increase of 0.3 percent in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage 
Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). 
Real average weekly earnings decreased 0.3 percent over the month due to the change in real average 
hourly earnings combined with a decrease of 0.3 percent in the average workweek.

U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services, September 2026
The U.S. Census Bureau and the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis announced today that the goods and services deficit was $105.0 billion in September, down $0.7 billion from $105.7 billion in August, revised.
U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services Deficit
 | Deficit: | $105.0 Billion | -0.7%°
 | Exports: | $321.5 Billion | +1.9%°
 | Imports: | $426.6 Billion | +1.2%°
 | 
Next release: Tuesday, December 8, 2026
(°) Statistical significance is not applicable or not measurable. Data adjusted for seasonality but not price changes
Source: U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis; U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services, November 4, 2026
Exports, Imports, and Balance (exhibit 1)
September exports were $321.5 billion, $5.8 billion more than August exports. September imports were $426.6 billion, $5.2 billion more than August imports.
The September decrease in the goods and services deficit reflected a decrease in the goods deficit of $0.7 billion to $135.9 billion and a decrease in the services surplus of less than $0.1 billion to $30.9 billion.
Year-to-date, the goods and services deficit decreased $92.4 billion, or 12.2 percent, from the same period in 2025. Exports increased $297.3 billion or 11.6 percent. Imports increased $204.9 billion or 6.2 percent.
Three-Month Moving Averages (exhibit 2)
The average goods and services deficit increased $11.3 billion to $101.2 billion for the three months ending in September.
Average exports increased $1.4 billion to $316.0 billion in September.
Average imports increased $12.7 billion to $417.2 billion in September.
Year-over-year, the average goods and services deficit increased $36.5 billion from the three months ending in September 2025.
Average exports increased $28.9 billion from September 2025.
Average imports increased $65.4 billion from September 2025.
Exports (exhibits 3, 6, and 7)
Exports of goods increased $5.1 billion to $211.0 billion in September.
 Exports of goods on a Census basis increased $5.0 billion.
Capital goods increased $3.8 billion.
Computers increased $1.3 billion.
Computer accessories increased $0.8 billion.
Civilian aircraft increased $0.7 billion.
Foods, feeds, and beverages increased $1.9 billion.
Soybeans increased $1.3 billion.
Consumer goods increased $0.8 billion.
Pharmaceutical preparations increased $0.7 billion.
Industrial supplies and materials decreased $1.0 billion.
Nonmonetary gold decreased $3.4 billion.
Crude oil increased $1.2 billion.
 Net balance of payments adjustments increased $0.1 billion.
Treatment of Gold in BEA’s International and National Economic Accounts
When incorporating the statistics in this release into BEA’s National Economic Accounts, including Gross Domestic Product, or GDP, BEA replaces exports and imports of nonmonetary gold with an adjustment calculated as the difference between domestic production and industrial use of gold. For additional information, see “How are exports and imports of gold recorded in BEA’s International Economic Accounts?” and “How are exports and imports of nonmonetary gold treated in BEA’s National Economic Accounts?”.
Exports of services increased $0.7 billion to $110.5 billion in September.
Travel increased $0.3 billion.
Charges for the use of intellectual property increased $0.1 billion.
Imports (exhibits 4, 6, and 8)
Imports of goods increased $4.4 billion to $346.9 billion in September.
 Imports of goods on a Census basis increased $8.0 billion.
Capital goods increased $11.6 billion.
Computers increased $7.6 billion.
Computer accessories increased $5.7 billion.
Semiconductors decreased $1.2 billion.

 Net balance of payments adjustments decreased $3.6 billion.
Imports of services increased $0.8 billion to $79.7 billion in September.
Travel increased $0.5 billion.
Transport increased $0.2 billion.
Real Goods in 2017 Dollars – Census Basis (exhibit 11)
The real goods deficit increased $3.5 billion, or 3.0 percent, to $119.5 billion in September, compared to a 2.2 percent increase in the nominal deficit. (The reason why the Census Basis nominal goods deficit increased, while the BOP nominal goods deficit decreased in September is attributable to a BOP adjustment for nonmonetary gold imports. See “How are exports and imports of gold recorded in BEA’s International Economic Accounts?”.)
Real exports of goods increased $0.2 billion, or 0.1 percent, to $152.2 billion, compared to a 2.5 percent increase in nominal exports.
Real imports of goods increased $3.6 billion, or 1.4 percent, to $271.6 billion, compared to a 2.4 percent increase in nominal imports.
Revisions
Revisions to August exports
Exports of goods were revised up $0.2 billion.
Exports of services were revised up $0.3 billion.
Revisions to August imports
Imports of goods were revised up $0.2 billion.
Imports of services were revised up $0.4 billion.
Goods by Selected Countries and Areas: Monthly – Census Basis (exhibit 19)
The September figures show surpluses, in billions of dollars, with Netherlands ($7.7), South and Central America ($6.2), United Kingdom ($3.0), Hong Kong ($2.5), Australia ($2.1), Brazil ($1.1), Singapore ($0.7), Saudi Arabia ($0.5), and Belgium ($0.2). Deficits were recorded, in billions of dollars, with Mexico ($28.7), Vietnam ($25.3), Taiwan ($21.9), China ($17.9), European Union ($14.2), South Korea ($12.2), Germany ($7.9), Italy ($6.3), Malaysia ($5.3), Japan ($4.8), India ($4.5), Canada ($4.4), Ireland ($3.0), Switzerland ($1.3), France ($1.3), and Israel ($0.7).
The deficit with Taiwan increased $3.6 billion to $21.9 billion in September. Exports increased $0.6 billion to $5.3 billion and imports increased $4.2 billion to $27.3 billion.
The deficit with the European Union increased $3.2 billion to $14.2 billion in September. Exports decreased $0.6 billion to $39.0 billion and imports increased $2.6 billion to $53.2 billion.
The deficit with Canada decreased $2.7 billion to $4.4 billion in September. Exports decreased $0.3 billion to $29.7 billion and imports decreased $3.0 billion to $34.1 billion.
All statistics referenced are seasonally adjusted; statistics are on a balance of payments basis unless otherwise specified. Additional statistics, including not seasonally adjusted statistics and details for goods on a Census basis, are available in exhibits 1-20b of this release. For information on data sources, definitions, and revision procedures, see the explanatory notes in this release. Explanatory Notes
Goods (Census basis)
Data for goods on a Census basis are compiled from the documents collected by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and reflect the movement of goods between foreign countries and the 50 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and U.S. Foreign Trade Zones. They include government and non-government shipments of goods and exclude shipments between the United States and its territories and possessions; transactions with U.S. military, diplomatic, and consular installations abroad; U.S. goods returned to the United States by its Armed Forces; personal and household effects of travelers; and in-transit shipments. The General Imports value reflects the total arrival of merchandise from foreign countries that immediately enters consumption channels, warehouses, or Foreign Trade Zones.
For imports, the value reported is the CBP-appraised value of merchandise—generally, the price paid for merchandise for export to the United States. Import duties, freight, insurance, and other charges incurred in bringing merchandise to the United States are excluded. The exception is exhibit 17a, which shows CIF import value. The CIF (cost, insurance, and freight) value represents the landed value of the merchandise at the first port of arrival in the United States. It is computed by adding import charges to the customs value and therefore excludes U.S. import duties.
Exports are valued at the f.a.s. (free alongside ship) value of merchandise at the U.S. port of export, based on the transaction price including inland freight, insurance, and other charges incurred in placing the merchandise alongside the carrier at the U.S. port of exportation.
Revision procedure (Census basis)
Monthly revisions: Monthly data include actual month's transactions as well as a small number of transactions for previous months. Each month, the U.S. Census Bureau revises the aggregate seasonally adjusted (nominal and real, or chained-dollar) and unadjusted export, import, and trade balance figures, as well as the end-use totals for the prior month. Country detail data and commodity detail data, based on the Standard International Trade Classification (SITC) Revision 4 and the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS), are not revised monthly. The timing adjustment shown in exhibit 14 is the difference between monthly data as originally reported and as recompiled.
For August 2026, unadjusted exports of goods were revised up $0.1 billion and unadjusted imports of goods were revised up $0.2 billion. Goods carry-over in September 2026 was $0.8 billion (0.4 percent) for exports and $0.4 billion (0.1 percent) for imports. For August 2026, revised export carry-over was less than $0.1 billion (less than 0.1 percent) and revised import carry-over was $0.1 billion (less than 0.1 percent).
Quarterly revisions to chain-weighted dollar series: For March, June, September, and December statistical month releases, revisions are made to the real, or chained-dollar, series presented in exhibits 10 and 11: the previous five months are revised to incorporate the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' (BLS) revisions to price indexes, which are used to produce the real series and to align Census data with data published by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) in the national income and product accounts (NIPAs).
Annual revisions: Each June, not seasonally adjusted goods data are revised to redistribute monthly data that arrived too late for inclusion in the month of transaction. In addition, revisions are made to reflect corrections received subsequent to the monthly revisions. Seasonally adjusted data are also revised to reflect

EMBARGOED UNTIL RELEASE AT 8:30 a.m. EDT, Thursday, October 29, 2026
 BEA 26—45
GDP (Advance Estimate), 3rd Quarter 2026
Real gross domestic product (GDP) increased at an annual rate of 3.4 percent in the third quarter of 2026 (July, August, and September), according to the advance estimate released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). In the second quarter, real GDP increased 2.2 percent.
The contributors to the increase in real GDP in the third quarter were increases in investment, consumer spending, and government spending that were partly offset by a decrease in exports. Imports, which are a subtraction in the calculation of GDP, increased. For more information, refer to the "Technical Notes" below.
Compared to the second quarter, the acceleration in real GDP in the third quarter primarily reflected an acceleration in investment and an upturn in government spending that were partly offset by a downturn in exports. Imports increased more in the third quarter than in the second quarter.
Real final sales to private domestic purchasers, the sum of consumer spending and gross private fixed investment, increased 4.9 percent in the third quarter, compared with an increase of 4.6 percent in the second quarter.
The price index for gross domestic purchases increased 3.0 percent in the third quarter, compared with an increase of 5.6 percent in the second quarter. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index increased 2.1 percent, compared with an increase of 5.0 percent, and the PCE price index, excluding food and energy increased 2.5 percent, compared with an increase of 3.3 percent.

Technical Notes
Sources of change for real GDP
Real GDP increased at an annual rate of 3.4 percent (0.8 percent at a quarterly rate 1) in the third quarter, reflecting increases in investment, consumer spending, and government spending that were partly offset by a decrease in exports. Imports, which are a subtraction in the calculation of GDP, increased.
More information on the source data and BEA assumptions that underlie the third-quarter estimate is shown in the key source data and assumptions table.
The increase in investment primarily reflected increases in private inventory investment and in equipment.
The largest contributors to the increase in private inventory investment were wholesale trade and manufacturing (both led by nondurable goods industries), based primarily on Census Bureau inventory book value data.
Within equipment, the increase was led by information processing equipment (mainly computers and peripheral equipment), based primarily on data for imports from the U.S. Census Bureau-BEA U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services report and the Census Bureau Advance Economic Indicators Report for September.
The increase in consumer spending reflected increases in both services and goods.
Within services, the increase was led by health care (mainly hospitals and outpatient services), based primarily on U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Current Employment Statistics, and food services and accommodations (mainly purchased meals and beverages), based on Census Bureau Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MRTS) data.
Within goods, the increase was led by other nondurable goods (mainly prescription drugs), based on Census Bureau MRTS data.
Within government spending, the increase was more than accounted for by federal government spending, led by nondefense consumption expenditures. The pattern of nondefense spending primarily reflected sales of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, based on data from the U.S. Department of Energy. Within the National Economic Accounts, sales are deducted from government consumption expenditures. In the third quarter, sales from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve were less than sales in the second quarter, resulting in an increase in consumption expenditures. Because the oil sold by the government is reflected as an increase in other components of GDP, there is no direct effect on GDP.
Exports and imports primarily reflected Census Bureau-BEA U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services data as well as the Census Bureau Advance Economic Indicators Report for September. The decrease in exports primarily reflected a decrease in goods (led by petroleum and related products). The largest contributor to imports was capital goods, except automotive.

Personal Income and Outlays, September 2026
Personal income increased $54.5 billion (0.2 percent at a monthly rate) in September, according to estimates released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). Disposable personal income (DPI)—personal income less personal current taxes—increased $52.7 billion (0.2 percent), and personal consumption expenditures (PCE) increased $113.1 billion (0.5 percent).
Personal outlays—the sum of PCE, personal interest payments, and personal current transfer payments—increased $113.0 billion in September. Personal saving was $911.1 billion, and the personal saving rate—personal saving as a percentage of DPI—was 3.8 percent.
The increase in current-dollar personal income in September primarily reflected increases in compensation and government social benefits.
The $113.1 billion increase in current-dollar PCE in September reflected increases of $35.1 billion in spending on goods and $78.1 billion in spending on services.
Real PCE increased $2.6 billion (less than 0.1 percent at a monthly rate) in September.
From the preceding month, the PCE price index for September increased 0.5 percent. Excluding food and energy, the PCE price index increased 0.3 percent.
From the same month one year ago, the PCE price index for September increased 3.6 percent. Excluding food and energy, the PCE price index increased 3.1 percent from one year ago.

 November 17, 2026 
How does EIA account for small differences between energy supply and demand data? 
Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Monthly Energy Review
Note: Supply = production + imports; demand = consumption + exports; demand - supply = stock change + other 
EIA uses over 60 surveys to collect data on the U.S. energy sector’s supply and demand. In theory, supply and demand should balance. In practice, we often have small differences between our total supply and total demand figures. 
To account for the differences between U.S. total primary energy supply and demand, our Monthly Energy Review includes a stock change and other data series, a grouping of items that account for the differences between supply and demand each month. 
These accounting differences represent a very small share of energy markets. In 2025, our combined surveys accounted for about 128 quadrillion British thermal units (quads) each for U.S. energy supply and demand, and stock change and other was 0.4 quads—about 0.3% of the total. 
Stock change is the net difference between energy held in storage at the beginning and end of a month. 
The other portion of stock change and other represents the many forms of small accounting differences: 
Differences in survey respondent accounting and reporting practices 
Differences in timing between energy activity occurrences and reporting periods 
Measurement and estimation errors 
Limitations in data collection systems and survey coverage 
Energy lost during transfers or storage 
Unreported energy activities 
To document the other differences between supply and demand, besides stock change, we use various adjustments, balancing items, and losses and unaccounted for series, a standard statistical accounting practice. Rather than indicating a flaw in the underlying statistics, these series ensure that published data are consistent and transparent, while also providing a measure of the uncertainty associated with our survey data. 
Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Monthly Energy Review
For petroleum and biofuels, our adjustments series accounts for the fact that survey responses may not precisely reflect actual activity. We’ve made improvements to our petroleum data over time to account for changes in transfers to crude oil supply, motor gasoline blending components, distillate fuel oil by pipeline operations, and other developments in petroleum markets. See Appendix B of our Petroleum Supply Monthly for more details. 
For natural gas, our balancing item series accounts for differences between supply and demand. Some of the differences are because of natural gas lost to the atmosphere. Also, there can be differences in conversions of flow data metered at varying temperatures and pressures, variations in company accounting and billing practices, and differences between billing cycles and calendar periods. See Appendix A of our Natural Gas Monthly for more details. 
For coal, we use a losses and unaccounted for series to represent differences in supply and demand, including coal lost during transport and various accounting and timing issues. In 2009, because of incomplete data coverage and different source data, biofuels have a small balancing item to balance biodiesel supply and demand.
